  • According to recent reports, making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic.
  • The secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

According to recent reports, making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

The secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

If you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

If you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

According to recent reports, while Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

The Scoop with Moynat’s Aydha Mehnaz: On Launching Her Fresh Consultancy Venture Avari

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week.
  • This week’s guest is Aydha Mehnaz, whose day job is head of global brand relations at Moynat, purveyor of trunks and the monogrammed totes your fashionable colleague started carrying around in the last couple of years.
  • Aydha with Paris Hilton at Mugler SS24 where Paris made her Paris runway debut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

This week’s guest is Aydha Mehnaz, whose day job is head of global brand relations at Moynat, purveyor of trunks and the monogrammed totes your fashionable colleague started carrying around in the last couple of years. I met Aydha when she worked in the PR department at Mugler, alongside Bertrand Le Gall (now the image director at Moynat), while I was at Selfridges. I remember it was the 30th anniversary of the brand’s Angel perfume that we were working on.

Aydha with Paris Hilton at Mugler SS24 where Paris made her Paris runway debut.

We hit it off because Aydha is cool and ambitious in all the right ways. She grew up in Bangladesh and studied biochemistry before leaving it all behind about 10 years ago for a Masters at ESMOD in Paris. From there, she landed at Mugler but, in between all that, she also started one of the first and best Tumblrs on modest fashion, called Minazification. The blog doesn’t work anymore, but Aydha very much does. She’s recently started a new venture, which is what we are talking about today.

I recently debuted Avari, my communications consultancy for brands and talent who want to reach the Southeastern consumer or Southeastern brands who want to do the opposite. I built it with my brother, who is based in Dhaka, because it was important for us to operate in four different time zones.

In a recent development, I come from Bangladesh but moved to Paris about 10 years ago, and now I am in New York. Throughout my career, while moving through those luxury spaces, I’ve been very conscious of how those places shape me, and Avari has the same geographical footprint as I do. The word in Sanskrit speaks to something that’s obscure, almost like a shapeshifter. Luxury no longer holds the same values it once did because the consumer has changed and has a more multicultural, constantly changing attitude.

Aydha with Jordan Clarkson of the NY Knicks during the Moynat Kasing Lung shoot.

In a recent development, we want to be a partner for brands and talents, making sure you can become whoever you want. For me, the main objective is to nurture talent from South Asia. There isn’t enough representation in Western media, and for those who are there, there isn’t enough guidance on how to package themselves to enter the Western market. There is so much talent coming from that part of the world, and particularly from Bangladesh since the July Uprising of 2024, but few know where to look or how. I do.

Talk to me about the difference between the Bangladesh you left as a student and the Bangladesh you are building a business for 10 years later.

When I left, the creative pool was quite small. There weren’t many people doing latest things; it was more iterations of what you would see from India or from Pakistan. Now there are so many designers, chefs, photographers, and all sorts of other artists who see themselves as global talents rather than being limited by their surroundings. This is why, for Avari, it was so key to set up a hub in Dhaka.

Aydha with guests attending at Moynat’s Travelling Popup in Chicago.

Sources indicate that you are the first Bangladeshi on the Scoop, so I have to ask you about the factory protests. What can you tell us about what is really happening on the ground?

It has been revealed that this is my very own observation, and I am not speaking for anyone, but protests are not newly introduced in Bangladesh or anywhere. Protests happen in Paris too, right? And the truth is always somewhere in the middle. In Bangladesh, you have a set of factories that are not regulated. They probably treat their workers very poorly and keep costs low by avoiding taking safety measures. But then you also have factories that are actually charging you a premium price, giving you the polo or the Carhartt sweatshirt you wear every day. This sweater I am wearing is actually made in Bangladesh.

So those factories are providing healthcare and safe facilities for their employees. The people who don’t get the right treatment are obviously going to protest. But the thing is that whenever these conversations take place in Western media, only one side, the bad side of Bangladesh, is shown. And there are also local people who profit from exacerbating that picture.

Does Bangladesh care about James Bond?

In a recent development, of course, the memes are crazy. I like the one about Robert Pattinson getting all the jobs.

It has been revealed that it’s interesting how much things have changed in 10-20 years. When I was growing up in Greece, global news didn’t have the same effect, whereas now we all see the same memes at the same time, everywhere. But we are all still culturally different.

Right, and that has affected how global consumers behave. As an example, Bangkok for the Bangladeshi is considered a second Dhaka — you literally walk on the street and run into people you know. Because the high earners from South Asia go to shop in Thailand, but also in India, the UAE, America, and Europe. South Asians have so many cultural similarities, and we often speak each other’s language too.

My introduction to luxury wasn’t the Western brands but my mum’s heirloom jewelry that she is waiting for me to inherit. We are talking about 24-karat pieces that have been passed down from generation to generation. You can see how a brand like Sabyasachi brings that into the modern world, and there are so many other local creatives with a global view. Locals are finally investing in South Asian culture and South Asian art. With Avari, the idea is: how do we fit into that?

According to recent reports, applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. Who would you like to see apply?

Industry observers note that khanums, a British label with Bangladeshi roots, and Menka from Bangladesh, who make these handwoven sarees with heirloom weavers. Also, Kartik Research from India is fab, but he’s already taken part.

Recent findings suggest that even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

Industry observers note that the Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Off-White x Nike Air Max 97 ‘White’.

In a recent development, some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

According to recent reports, arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

Air Jordan 1 High OG ‘Yin Yang’.

Recent findings suggest that the Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

We’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

A version of the story originally appeared on British GQ.

Tech Report: Wig Business Is Massive Business

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hair category is currently a hotbed for growth.
  • Recent findings suggest that after 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Full hair has always been in style,” says Charlotte Mensah.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hair category is currently a hotbed for growth. Alongside much innovation in existing products, the past decade has seen hair transplants, scalp serums, and novel treatment concepts like head spas surge in popularity. And the category holds appeal across many demographics, from the more traditional mid-life market to burgeoning legions of ‘looksmaxxers’ and ever younger consumers seeking interventions for early-stage thinning, pattern baldness and GLP1-induced hair loss. While many consumers are investing in supplements, serums or aesthetic treatments to address the problem, another cohort is spending significant on extensions and wigs.

Recent findings suggest that after 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal. “Even with my clients that embrace their natural look, many are seeing value in adding volume/length and will request a weft that matches their hair texture to achieve this,” she explains. What’s more, extensions and wigs have become less of a secret, considered desirable across race, gender and other consumer groups. “The appearance of full, healthy hair is always fashionable. These days, we have new methods like tapes and synthetic fibers that can simulate human hair, making hair extensions more accessible to everyone,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that “Full hair has always been in style,” says Charlotte Mensah. “I’ve noticed clients are increasingly interested in extensions that mirror their hair’s natural texture.”.

As revenues go, the wig business is a lucrative business. The SKUs in this sector — wigs, wefts and other hair extension systems, such as lace toupees and semi-permanent, bonded K-tips — commonly necessitate multibuy purchases to achieve desired hairstyles and individually command price tags upwards of £250.

According to recent reports, at the top end of the market, a single wig or set of extensions can sell for tens of thousands, with long extension lengths, made-to-measure customizations and laborious finishes justifying costs. Value perception is high, thanks to human hair’s product lifespan, reusability and styling versatility. Together with growing hair loss concerns, these factors encourage consumers to adopt an investment-purchase mindset that makes for higher average order values in the extensions space.

Having earned £20,000 through 30 orders in just 10 minutes on launch day, CEO Denise Nwogbu has honed a strategy for success here. Her wig brand Go Glueless positions its product offer as a “hair appointment in a box”, eliminating the friction associated with installing specialist extensions. Customers are drawn to the convenience and seamless nature of the wigs, which do not require adhesives to style — instead, they can be secured through elastic headbands on the wig’s interior that keep it fitted in place on the user’s scalp. She indicates this ease of installation has driven high waitlist demand and often results in sellouts across the range on drop days.

Denise Nwogbu, CEO and founder of Go Glueless, has found success positioning her product as a “salon appointment in a box.”.

“We limit releases to four times a year and use a pre-order model. This allows time to carefully source single-donor, virgin hair, then handcraft and customize each bespoke unit,” Nwogbu shares. “Provenance is everything — I chose my supplier in Vietnam because she has a real relationship with each woman who grows and sells their hair for the production of the extensions. She does not delegate to hair collectors, she goes personally to the villages to find willing volunteers that have not been coerced into cutting their hair. She can tell you their exact age, name and lifestyle, and pays them fairly with an understanding of virgin hair value in the West.”.

Recent findings suggest that by the time the hair reaches Go Glueless headquarters in Birmingham, it has been cuticle-tested to ensure quality and longevity. Then, a team of wig specialists construct, color and cut units to exact customer measurements. Attracting an affluent, often time-poor clientele of professional women and public figures, Go Glueless’s USP lies in doing the labor so the end consumer has it completely removed.

On launch day, Go Glueless made £20,000 in online preorders. Now, the brand has opened its first IRL space —a suite where customers can browse and get bespoke fittings for their wigs.

In a recent development, “It’s a salon experience with no skills needed, but education is also important: every customer gets access to exclusive tutorials through GG Academy, our online portal,” Denise says. This in itself is a clever strategy, attracting large audiences already searching for terms like “wig install tutorial”, which has amassed 478,000 impressions on TikTok. “And we educate our clients about help available to them if they are buying wigs to manage medical hair loss — many with conditions like alopecia or cancer aren’t aware of their entitlement to VAT relief.”.

It has been revealed that in the wig business, hair loss sufferers are likely to be engaged, repeat customers, presenting major sales opportunities. But profits aren’t the only piece of the puzzle — the most impactful brands focus on corporate social responsibility, too.

Sources indicate that market leader Beauty Works, whose assortment includes both professional-grade extensions and DIY clip-ins, is a case in point. Its relationship with the charity Little Lady Locks, which provides free medical wigs and hair services to minors with medical hair loss, is symbiotic: the charity benefits from Beauty Works’s financial investment, resources and expert volunteers, while Beauty Works can exhibit purpose-driven values, benefiting from enhanced brand image and positive engagement within aligned communities.

Beauty Works donates hair extensions to Little Lady Locks, helping the charity provide free wigs to boost the confidence of hair loss sufferers under 18.

In a recent development, elsewhere, the brand is massive on avoiding ethical quandaries common to the hair trade by enforcing strict compliance throughout its supply chain. “Our human hair is voluntarily sold by individuals who are fairly compensated,” says Randilyn Dela Cruz, product architect and vice president of development at Beauty Works’ parent tech giant BIG. “Our sourcing standards require a respectful process and prohibit child labor, forced labor and sourcing from regions where there are known human-rights violations,” she details.

Sourcing is an important aspect for any wig business to get right, especially given a black market of sorts exists. A far cry from the luxury products they’re promoted as in the West, some vendors acquire hair of dubious origin, obscure its imperfections and sell to unwitting customers overseas at a high markup. An ITV News exposé found this can include waste hair pulled from sewer drains in India, as well as “floor hair” collected from the ground of salons by cheap laborers desperate to cash in on the lucrative trade.

“It’s ‘the fast fashion’ side of wigs,” Denise stresses, going on to explain that these vendors chemically relax the waste balls of hair — which are made up of several cut hairs with different properties because they are from multiple donors’ heads — to the point where it appears flawless. “They often then market it deceptively under names like ‘bone straight’. “You couldn’t tell with the naked eye, but when you use that kind of hair to produce hair extensions, time always tells. It frizzes up, tangles easily and is unpredictable after the chemical coatings wash off, and business owners risk having that happen in the hands of your consumer if you don’t do your due diligence at the point of sourcing,” she warns.

It has been revealed that hence, Denise insists on flying to Vietnam personally to inspect and test the quality of any hair used in the making of Go Glueless units. It’s expensive work, but something she recommends as worthwhile for latest businesses hoping to break into the luxury wig space.

Another common source of hair that can pose ethical dilemmas is Indian temple hair. This hair comes from Hindu tonsuring ceremonies, in which some donors shave their heads under the religious belief that it releases past spiritual baggage. Others agree to shed their hair as a sacred sacrifice to be devoted to specific deities. These individuals are often left in the dark about the final destination of their hair and its huge monetary value if it is later sold on to wig companies at auction, and they often receive no part of the profits, according to a recent report from the BBC. Questions around exploitation in these cases can influence perception among discerning end consumers, and are worth investigating to reduce brand risk.

Model wears Synths 2: an extension that uses collagen-based fibers to add length and volume without the need for human hair or more toxic synthetic alternatives.

In a recent development, to sidestep sourcing concerns entirely, Charlotte Mensah often opts for “man-made fibers that have been designed to perform like human hair and that can still be styled with heat tools” in her salon. This is an area of category expansion, with synthetic products from Outré reaching viral fame and plant-based hair brands like Rebundle, Knott and Ruka Hair attracting new audiences with innovative alternatives to traditional human hair extensions.

Ruka Hair’s latest invention (a plastic-free, collagen-based braiding fiber called Synths 2) became the first-ever hair extension of its kind to land in Sephora doors this summer. Stockist support of this caliber affirms it: the wig business is major business indeed, and with the right sourcing, can set savvy founders up for exponential growth.

Tech Report: What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don't Need to Go in the Oven?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook.
  • On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey.
  • Industry observers note that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here.

On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed.

Industry observers note that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bull’s-eye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked.

The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place.

With that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three, episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful.

Sources indicate that but you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it.

Industry observers note that green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better.

Green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly.

Industry observers note that brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible!

Air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds.

In a recent development, sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done promptly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.”.

Sources indicate that glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here.

Parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright.

According to recent reports, adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori.

It has been revealed that kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here.

Recent findings suggest that instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too.

Readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments!

Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

#20018. As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release.
  • Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child.
  • It has been revealed that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first newly introduced installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, quickly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

It has been revealed that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

Recent findings suggest that I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

It has been revealed that by the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

Recent findings suggest that the third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a new city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between fresh installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that highlights videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

Recent findings suggest that after several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It says so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

It has been revealed that start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

Once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party. Make them the day before the party, pop them (tightly wrapped or in an airtight container!) into the fridge, and forget about them until ready to serve.

#20015. Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1509 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).
  • It has been revealed that however, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly introduced Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66).
  • Industry observers note that “Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).

It has been revealed that however, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly introduced Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66). While merch is nothing fresh in the fashion market — Balenciaga relied heavily on it during Demna’s tenure between 2015 and 2025 — the playing field is changing, with a stronger focus on the temporal buzz of a new digital or game-based craze, the cult movie everyone’s watching, the fiendishly anticipated alt-rap tour, or a new milestone in a girl-boss beauty community’s trajectory — like Rhode founder Hailey Bieber’s 30th birthday.

Industry observers note that “Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle. But with [consumers] suddenly coveting more transient ‘merchandise’ over main line product ranges, is that investment misplaced?” asks Simon Richardson, group strategy director at creative agency Amplify. “What [brands] should be doing is creating a moment in time, not just a product line. Fans need more — all the time — to signal what they care about in a way that feels distinct, real and truly of a moment.”.

Outside the Selfridges GTA launch.

In a recent development, recently, Jordan Firstman, director of buzzy gay drama Club Kid, called on New York designer Emily Dawn Long — renowned among Dimes Square it-kids for her in-the-know screenprinted vintage tees — to design the merch for the film. The designer, known for her Spoiled Boys slogan tee, emblazoned the ragged tops with one of the film’s lines, “It’s like that every time”. In the film itself, Firstman also wore his own Emily Dawn Long tee, printed with the words, “Take off your clothes”. On Wednesday, A24 took over a downtown 1<3 NY souvenir shop to sell the capsule, before releasing a limited online drop (most styles are sold out).

A24 worked with designer Emily Dawn Long for fresh film Club Kid’s merch.

It has been revealed that tech bros are also tapping in. This year, Trump-contracted data surveillance firm Palantir released a chore jacket ($239) not dissimilar to those purveyed by cult restaurants, such as Sessions Arts Club and St. John. Reportedly, the organization’s broader apparel line is performing, especially in South Korea, where the windbreaker ($170) sold out. Much-talked-about corporation Nvidia — whose CEO Jensen Huang stepped down this week following his extramarital affair with a potential Chinese spy — also released a sweater emblazoned with a leather-jacketed cartoon of Huang ($178). The design is picking up strong resale value again following the scandal: one seller listed the design on Ebay for $2,500. And OpenAI offers a racing-style shirt ($75) not dissimilar to styles from Corteiz, Palace and Supreme — as well as bumper stickers ($10) and caps ($40), all sold on its website.

It has been revealed that as luxury struggles to justify its price hikes — since the average price of personal luxury goods increased by 52% between 2019 and 2024, per HSBC — the merch market has swooped in to capitalize on the aspirational shopper. In the US, consumer sentiment is low, and yet spending is up. Indeed, across the US, Europe and China, shoppers are more cautious and discerning with discretionary purchases, guided by a brand’s value propositions. If a band tee, a Roblox hoodie, or a pair of GTA x Travis Scott Nike Air Force 1 sneakers can communicate cultural belonging, community adjacency, and lifestyle for a fraction of the cost of a luxury handbag, then merch wins.

Indeed, in late 2025, 72% of Gen Z luxury shoppers told Vogue Business they would prefer owning a Walmart “Wirkin” over a genuine Hermès Birkin, and when interviewed, several respondents said they deem spending lots of money on luxury distasteful and that luxury goods are not worth the cost. At the same time, beauty continues to boom with aspirational shoppers, but — unlike clothing and accessories — has only a handful of ways to turn its goods into walking advertisements. The Rhode phone case, seen in influencer selfies, marked the first step towards a solution, then came the wearable merch. Similarly, tech giants largely deal in intangible goods. But physical merch is a way for fans to display their favorite chip-maker or AI platform.

Hailey Bieber wears her latest Rhode windbreaker, which retails at $257.

Sources indicate that for beauty, and even tech, merch gives brand fans a way to express their appreciation of the products and the communities around them. Companies recognize young people’s appetite to feel part of something.

It has been revealed that millennial readers will remember when “merch” referred primarily to band T-shirts. That playbook began in musical subcultures and has now transferred to a broader market. “Gen Alpha grew up inside worlds. For them, a ‘skin’ [Fortnite’s in-game outfits] is merch, a creator’s snack bar is merch, and a hoodie is the physical version of a world they already spend hours in,” says Jolyon Varley, co-founder of marketing agency OK Cool.

Recent findings suggest that “Logos used to confer status and were a more reliable indicator of what you could afford or how you were living,” he adds. “Merch tells people what you’re into, and that’s become far more valuable. It’s a matter of signaling taste rather than wealth.”.

Varley points to the frenzy seen at GTA’s Selfridges launch, explaining that consumers now associate with much more than simply products, but instead entire worlds. “GTA isn’t just a game any more,” he claims. “Millions of people live in it. The launch week proved it.”.

Whether that’s an event exclusive, an IP artefact made real for the ‘heads’, or even a staff uniform, exclusivity and experience are major drivers of hype, says Amplify’s Richardson. “Something that says, ‘I was there’, not just ‘this is what I’m into’.”.

Richardson also notes that fandom thrives on shared codes and signals. So his advice for brands wanting a piece of the pie? “Bringing together your own lore, something that anchors your merch in time, and the right collaborators to bring it to life in a fan-first and agile way, can turn a small run of products into a mass-reach driver.” The Rockstar Games’s GTA takeover of Miami — a reported $3.9 million deal with Miami-Dade County — sets the bar, lighting up Miami Heat’s stadium, dressing players in black-and-pink jerseys, and activating across the city.

Merch’s appeal lies in the power of the brand and what that communicates. It’s a quick win to cross categories, too. “If you build a brand that is cool, interesting, culturally relevant, aspirational, it [almost] doesn’t matter what you’re selling, because what you’re selling is the aura — this ineffable, ‘it’, cool factor,” indicates Ursula founder and brand strategist Emma Hope Allwood. “Just practically, when you have these massive cultural moments or releases like GTA, it makes sense to try to break it down into different categories — different ways for people to be part of it, rather than it just being a game.”.

It has been revealed that luxury brands that want to re-enter the merch market and cultural players looking to seize the growing momentum need to broach the sector carefully. “Not all merch is cool,” claims Sara McAlpine, co-founder of brand and marketing studio Bikini, highlighting the recent tech brand plays. “There’s no reason to be producing a chore coat unless you’re trying to say you’re aligned with a Carhartt WIP and Japanese-denim wearing aesthetic-conscious crowd.”.

Industry observers note that so what works? Influencer and DJ Leo Mandella visited the GTA Selfridges pop-up. He typically doesn’t consider merch cool — “[it] can look a bit gimmicky” — but the capsule delivered, he believes. “It’s very easy for gaming companies to mess up on the rest of the promo run, but Rockstar were absolutely incredible at creating a capsule of merch that was just as good as the game,” claims Mandella, who spent £250 (roughly $329) at the pop-up. “I think merch is especially exciting when done well because you feel part of a moment. It’s not just a piece of clothing. Buying a Vice City tee or a Burger Shot uniform [the official in-game restaurant chain] makes you feel like you’re in this fictional world.”.

Inside the Selfridges GTA activation.

According to recent reports, nonetheless, for brands that still want to communicate esotericism, merch remains an astute method. Varley pinpoints the power of releasing one-off, friends-and-family T-shirts during events. He cites the Awake x Jordan T-shirts — art directed by London graffiti artist Fatzoo — given out during Notting Carnival at the Deviation stage. “That immediately orients you in a specific nucleus of that scene,” he says. “If you weren’t there — or don’t know the individuals involved — you didn’t get one.”.

This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November.
  • It has been revealed that zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market.
  • It has been revealed that that’s true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

It has been revealed that zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that upcoming business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta said. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”.

It has been revealed that that’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Firm, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy said. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all quickly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

It has been revealed that when it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the new onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also launched this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

That watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta said they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”.

In the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us fresh clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”.

Zenith created irresistible bait for this upcoming stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

The dials of the latest collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

Zenith intends to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

Industry observers note that with the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are currently booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.
