  • If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright.
  • Recent findings suggest that but it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s nothing quite like a Christmas market to set a joyful tone for the holiday season. Is there anywhere else where it’s acceptable to mill about with a hearty mug of glögg in one hand, an even larger potato pancake in the other, while exceeding your budget on handcrafted ornaments and posing for photos in front of a wooden sleigh? The answer, we can confidently say, is no.

If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright. A natural place to start when curating an itinerary is Germany, and for good reason: It is, after all, the birthplace of the Christmas market, with Dresden’s Striezelmarkt first springing up all the way back in 1434.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event. There are numerous other destinations scattered across the continent—some familiar, and some wonderfully under the radar—that deliver the festive goods. Here, find 22 storybook European Christmas markets to make 2026 your most memorable holiday season yet.

What to Expect: The Stortorget Christmas Market is held in Gamla Stan, Stockholm’s old town, that dates back to the 13th century and is encircled by historic merchant houses. It’s often snowy this time of year, so enjoy the crunch of fresh powder beneath your feet as you meander medieval alleys and peruse the market’s 41 chalet-shaped stalls. If you’re hungry, pick up a smoked sausage or some lussekatter, a brioche-like saffron bun. You can cross everyone off your shopping list with the cozy selection of hand-knitted sweaters and traditional ornaments, all illuminated by the market’s endless strings of festive lights. (And speaking of light, if your visit to Stockholm happens to land on December 13, don’t miss Lucia, the country’s traditional, candlelit festival.).

Where to Stay: Lydmar Hotel (12-minute walk).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: The term ‘fairytale’ gets thrown around a lot when speaking of Christmas markets, but in the case of Wroclaw, it’s simply the best way to describe it. This magical atmosphere—complete with gothic architecture and a 75-foot-tall (artificial!) Norwegian spruce—stretches across four interconnected areas: the market square (Rynek), the salt square (Plac Solny), Świdnicka Street, and Oławska Street. While exploring, don’t miss the opportunity to try oscypek, a smoked cheese from the Polish mountains that is served with cranberries and best paired with a glass of mead (Poland’s oldest traditional alcoholic drink).

Where to Stay: Hotel Altus Palace (15-minute walk).

Location: Place des Dominicains, Place Jeanne d’Arc, Place de l’Ancienne Douanne, Koïfhus, Place des Six Montagnes Noires, and Square de la Montagne Verte.

When: Ends December 29 (though the Gourmet Market runs until January 3).

According to recent reports, what to Expect: There are six (yes, six) total markets in this little town, which looks like the missing chapter of a fairytale book even when it’s not covered in string lights and fir branches. They’re all scattered around the Old Town and serve slightly different purposes: The main one on Place des Dominicains is mostly arts and crafts themed, with a few kids’ rides spread; the Place Jeanne d’Arc market is set up to look like a traditional Alsatian village; the Marché Gourmand at Square de la Montagne Verte is the spot for scrapings of creamy raclette, rich tartiflette, and hot cups of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Relais & Châteaux La Maison Des Têtes (3-minute walk).

What to Expect: Dating back to the 17th century, the Nuremberg Christmas market (“Christkindlesmarkt”) is one of the first on the continent, and the city certainly goes all-out in homage to this tradition. Nicknamed the “city of wood and cloth,” it stands out for its candy cane-striped cloth tents, each housing glass tree baubles, fresh-baked gingerbread, and handmade wooden trinkets. Traveling with little ones? The children’s Christmas market is just around the corner on Hans-Sachs-Platz, and includes everything from a lit-up merry-go-round to a bake house where they can roll out their own dough.

Where to Stay: Karl August (one-minute walk).

Location: On Barfüsserplatz and Münsterplatz in the historic old town.

What to Expect: In Basel, around 155 rustic wooden chalets are set against the backdrop of the city’s old town, set aglow with glittering lights. A magnificent Christmas tree is erected in the historic center with ornaments by local decorating legend Johann Wanner, while stalls are bedecked in string lights and tinsel at every turn. After picking up a few artisanal gifts and goodies, head for the 13-meter-high Christmas pyramid on Barfüsserplatz for mulled wine, followed by a stroll along the Rhine River.

Where to Stay: Les Trois Rois (10-minute walk).

What to Expect: The Wiener Chriskindlemarkt und Weihnachtstraum Christmas market is perhaps the largest and well-known in Vienna, but with this precedent comes crowds. Instead, founder of bespoke travel organization Black Tomato Tom Marchant points to the Christmas village at the Belvedere Palace as an in-the-know, less-trafficked alternative preferred by locals; here, you can wander around the palace’s lavish 18th-century Baroque architecture while indulging in mulled wine and delectable pastries. “Lots of locally crafted jewelry can be found in this area,” claims Marchant. “Scented woods, ceramics, wooden hats, decorations, drinking horns—it’s quite a stunning place.”.

Where to Stay: Miiro Spittelberg (20 minutes by tram).

Location: The Grande Île (Old Town).

What to Expect: Known by holiday devotees as the “capital of Christmas,” Strasbourg is home to the oldest holiday market in France, dating all the way back to 1570. Visitors to this picturesque city in the Alsace region can pop in and out of 13 quaint markets, all within walking distance of each other in the old town. The original, however, is known as Christkindelsmärik and can be found at Place Broglie—there you, can sip on a mug of vin chaud while zipping around tinsel-adorned chalets in front of the Gothic cathedral.

Where to Stay: Hotel Cour du Corbeau Strasbourg-Mgallery (15-minute walk).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: Christmas markets and Germany are inextricably linked—it’s been estimated that there are over 2,500 in the country alone—and one of the best places to begin your exploration of the region’s holiday traditions is in the fairytale fortress town of Heidelberg. The historic city’s landscape includes the Neckar River and Odenwald Forest, while it also boasts architectural landmarks such as the Old Bridge and a prestigious 14th-century university attended by everyone from Hegel to Hannah Arendt. Heidelberg’s Christmas market is scattered throughout the illuminated storybook alleys of the old town, where the smell of roasted nuts wafts in the air as you dip into huts for souvenirs. Kids in tow? Go ice skating on Karlsplatz, or take a spin on the antique carousel.

Where to Stay: Heidelberg Suites House of Hütter (10-minute walk).

Where to Stay: Telegraaf Hotel (5-minute walk).

Location: East Princes Street Garden.

What to Expect: With the unmistakable silhouettes of Edinburgh Castle and the Scott Monument in the distance, Edinburgh’s holiday market—located in the center of the Scottish city—imbues its ancient walkways with a lively charm. Take in bird’s eye views from atop the glittering ferris wheel or glide across the ice skating rink surrounded by 18th-century architecture. Afterward, trot around the cheery network of vendors serving Scottish delicacies and winter drinks, or pick up last-minute artisanal gifts and decorations at the market’s many boutique stalls.

Where to Stay: The Roseate Edinburgh (10-minute drive).

Location: Tivoli Gardens and Højbro Plads.

When: Ends January 3 and December 20, respectively.

Industry observers note that what to Expect: Entering Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens during the holiday season feels like wandering into an undiscovered Nordic village. This 175-year-old theme park is transformed annually into a Christmas market with 60 stalls swathed in magical decor, including log cabins draped in pine cones and layers of snow—and that’s without mentioning the garden itself, which glows with over 70,000 Christmas baubles and 1,000-plus trees draped in lights. A 10-minute walk away, Højbro Plads also lures in visitors with 18,000 sparkling lights, plus live reindeer pulling a Santa’s sleigh.

Where to Stay: Villa Copenhagen (5 and 15-minute walk).

Sources indicate that what to Expect: If you’re looking for a more pastoral feel, head to the Cotswolds, England’s most romantic region of storybook countryside. “With quaint villages adorned in lights, caroling, and frequent dustings of snow, the Cotswolds evokes Christmas from the days of old,” Marchant says. The ancient city of Bath sits on the region’s edge and is hosting the 20th anniversary of its annual holiday market this year. With over 150 stalls offering unique goods like pottery, hand-knit socks, artisan cheeses, and beyond, you’ll cross off your shopping list—and then some.

Where to Stay: Thyme (1-hour drive).

Location: Govone Castle and Asti’s historic center.

What to Expect: Bordering France and Switzerland, Italy’s northern Piedmont region is a hotspot for wintry festivities—but the atmospheric Christmas markets of neighboring towns Govone and Asti are the real standout. In Govone, tucked away inside the 18th-century royal castle, is both the House of Santa Claus and an exhibition that timelines the city’s Christmas celebrations over the centuries. If you want to shop, however, nearby Asti is where you’ll find over 130 workstations of artisans and food and wine producers scattered across Italy; afterwards, visit the living nativity scene put on by nearly 100 local volunteers.

Where to Stay: Relais San Maurizio (30-minute drive).

In a recent development, what to Expect: If you ask Finns where Santa Claus comes from, they’ll proudly declare their country as the answer. (Lapland, to be precise.) This alone makes celebrating the holiday in the capital of Helsinki an exhilarating and celebratory affair. “This is one of the best holiday markets in Europe,” Marchant says. “The cathedral overlooks the Helsinki Christmas market, which has over 100 stalls and stands with hand-crafted gifts, ornaments, locally-grown produce, and fish and meats sourced hyper-locally.” What are you waiting for?

Where to Stay: Hotel Haven (5-minute walk).

Industry observers note that location: Vorosmarty Square and St. Stephen’s Basilica.

It has been revealed that what to Expect: Brave the bone-chilling weather with a bowl of goulash soup or steaming chimney cake at Budapest’s beloved Christmas market located along the cobblestone streets of Vörösmarty Tér (Vorosmarty Square) in the heart of the city. About a 10-minute walk away you can also discover Christmas festivities in front of St. Stephen’s Basilica; the advent festival hosts around 100 craft exhibitors, an ice rink, and more. (It was named Best Christmas Market in Europe for three years in a row, if that sort of accolade piques your interest.).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest (5-minute walk).

In a recent development, what to Expect: This century-old holiday fair has over 100 wooden stalls and is nestled in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor town square. The merrymaking vibes are cemented with a glowing carousel, nativity scenes (belénes), and loads of handcrafted ornaments and gifts to choose from. You can also savor seasonal Spanish flavors like churros con chocolate washed down with a cup of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Villa Magna (15-minute drive).

Location: Market Square and Simon Stevin Square.

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: Appointed the whimsical title of Winter Glow, the annual festival in the medieval city of Bruges is nothing short of magical. Begin your visit on the light trail; a walk along 10 illuminated installations, all connected by a wintry blue glow. Then head for the Christmas markets for festivities that feel plucked from a fairytale. Technically there are two markets—one in the Market Square and the other in Simon Stevin Square—but as they are situated less than a five-minute walk from each other, it’s easy to do both. Peruse the atmospheric stalls for handcrafted decorations, wool socks, and plenty of Belgian treats and mulled wine, followed by a spin around the ice rink.

Where to Stay: Hotel Van Cleef (10-minute walk).

Location: Roßmarkt, along the Zeil, down to Römerberg, and to the Main River.

What to Expect: With origins dating back to the 14th century, the Frankfurt Christmas market is among the oldest in the world. As such, it’s also one of the most popular markets, attracting millions of festive guests each year and stretching across several parts of the old town. Meander through its many decorated stalls, make a pitstop at the tree in Römerberg square, and don’t forget to devour a bethmännchen (a marzipan pastry that is unique to Frankfurt and baked just for Christmas).

Where to Stay: Schlosshotel Kronberg (30-minute drive).

Location: Dom and Residenzplatz Square.

What to Expect: This traditional market is cozied up in the heart of Salzburg’s UNESCO World Heritage Site and has origins that go back to the late 15th century. These days, Christmas lovers descend upon the market’s 100-plus stands in search of Austrian specialties, festive incense aromas, traditional crafts, and decorations for the tree—all found within traditional huts.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Schloss Fuschl (30-minute drive).

Location: Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square.

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: Soak up the magic of Czechia at Prague’s holiday market. Get into the spirit of the season as you hop from one decorated wooden hut to the next, purchasing artisan crafts and delectable treats along the way. Curious what you’ll be eating? Look to popular Czech dishes like šunka (big hams roasted on spits), klobása (barbecued sausages), and rybí polévka (a traditional Christmas soup).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Prague (10 to 20 minute walk).

What to Expect: For those in search of something out of the ordinary, Valkenburg’s underground Christmas markets are a winning bet. The small southern Dutch town hits all the marks when it comes to setting the right tone for the season, but once you head into its caves and tunnels that’s when the magic truly begins. Bedecked in twinkly lights, these merry passages wind beneath castle ruins and offer stalls stocked with gifts and goodies. There’s even a cave with life-size sand sculptures and 3-D holiday paintings. Above ground, pay a visit to Santa’s Village, a more traditional market filled with chalets serving up hot drinks and Christmas trinkets.

It has been revealed that where to Stay: Château St. Gerlach (10-minute drive).

Where to Stay: Amerikalinjen (10-minute walk).

#19995. BA's Best Pecan Pie

BA's Best Pecan Pie

📅 12 Nov 2016 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients.
  • Recent findings suggest that brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust.

Recent findings suggest that brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard.

Recent findings suggest that when the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup?

It has been revealed that yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture.

For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie.

Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves?

Sources indicate that yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven.

Can I make pecan pie ahead of time?

In a recent development, yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months.

Industry observers note that pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough).

Turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour.

Industry observers note that preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

In a recent development, line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool.

Industry observers note that reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust.

In a recent development, bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

According to recent reports, with the space aglow in Ferrari Rosso Scuderia red under a shiny mirrored disco ball and a checkered-flag DJ booth, guests snacked on wagyu bites and gourmet caviar-topped chicken nuggets and sipped on-theme cocktails. (Also served: SkinCeuticals’s top-shelf favorites, including the P-TIOX and C E Ferulic serums, passed around on silver trays.) The model Kelly Piquet, partner of F1 star Max Verstappen, posted up on the green velvet banquette, as other attendees played around with SkinCeuticals-branded poker chips and cards around the room.

According to recent reports, on the venue’s outdoor terrace overlooking the glowing marvel that is Sphere, actor Chace Crawford and his dad, dermatologist Chris Wayne Crawford, took a moment to enjoy the view. The two were doing a little father-son bonding—a perfect setting since F1 is “a male, testosterone-fueled sport,” joked Chris. As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” said the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

Inside, sportscaster and former Seattle Seahawk superstar Russell Wilson, a major F1 fan, couldn’t wait for lights-out-and-away-we-go on Sunday. He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he said, “so I’m fired up about it.”.

At 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. When the musician Sooin, of the K-pop group Meovv, hopped into the booth to chop it up with the Chainsmokers, the room lit up.

They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.

“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”.

Chace Crawford and Chris Wayne Crawford.

Latest Update: Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Industry observers note that cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

According to recent reports, reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

In a recent development, using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

In a recent development, remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

Breaking: KFC Franchisee Files For Bankruptcy With 84 Locations At Risk Of Closure

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (321 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy.
  • In a recent development, the firm entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum!
  • It has been revealed that in its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy. The operator, Tasty Chick’n, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Texas on November 16.

In a recent development, the firm entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum! Brands. Tasty Chick’n’s portfolio includes 75 KFC restaurants and nine co-branded locations across Tennessee, Florida, Virginia, Arkansas, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, Alabama, Mississippi, and Indiana.

It has been revealed that in its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, restaurant-level profit margins have dropped to just 4 percent, down from 11 percent in 2023. And under its franchise agreements, nearly half of the franchisees’ locations require substantial and expensive upgrades through 2029.

Recent findings suggest that tasty Chick’n began deferring royalty payments in mid-2025 and generally stopped paying them altogether that November. This past September, KFC and Taco Bell’s franchising entities issued a notice of intent to terminate their agreements, claiming the operator owed nearly $16 million in unpaid royalties and other fees. Tasty Chick’n also faces approximately 14 lawsuits from landlords in five states over unpaid rent and other charges. The bankruptcy filing revealed that the operator has accrued nearly $73 million in funded debt.

The fate of the restaurants remains undecided. Tasty Chick’n is planning a court-supervised sale of its portfolio, either in its entirety or divided into different regional markets. Whether buyers will bite is another story, especially given KFC’s overall trajectory. A report earlier this year revealed that KFC had shuttered more than 300 locations between July 2025 and July 2026 alone.

No matter what happens to these KFC locations, this bankruptcy is another reminder of just how tough 2026 has been for fast food operators.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you book something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

Recent findings suggest that there are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

Our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

It has been revealed that for a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator.

Industry observers note that exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost.

Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

We’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, elevator, coffee maker, building staff.

When you want to head out for dinner, you’re spoilt for choice—but start with Chez Nenesse, a classic, red-and-white checkered tablecloth bistrot, that’s just four minutes away.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer, Bose sound system, indoor fireplace, coffee maker.

The building itself is listed as a historic monument dating back to the 17th century, and interior highlights like a painted ceiling and gilded mirror amplify the antique appeal. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

Here, rustic wood beams accent nearly every ceiling and wall, textured brick flooring adds warmth, and a large, tiled tub looks out onto Haussmannian rooftops for a truly cozy stay. It even has two balconies—sure, they may be tiny, but the sweeping views of the city’s architecture more than makes up for their size.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, television, piano, balcony, bathtub.

Best for: Those looking for a non-traditional vacation rental.

Sources indicate that A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. It’s deceptively spacious—thanks to a sofa bed, it can actually sleep up to six people—making it ideal for a girls’ trip to the city. With a spacious living area and a well-equipped kitchen, it’s certainly designed to handle a larger group. A nice bonus? You’re within walking distance of the beloved bookstore Shakespeare and Manufacturer for a souvenir you can employ on the long flight home.

Amenities: Kitchen, TV, fireplace, washer/dryer, bathtub.

(The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

This literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Recent findings suggest that combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Sources indicate that add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

Industry observers note that broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

The Hottest Thing in Nordic Design Right Now? The Vikings

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships.
  • Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.
  • “Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” states Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norway is a country built on craftsmanship.

Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships. (Not to mention wool, linen, and leather for their unheralded colorful attire.).

Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.

Traditional wool weaving at Viking Valley.

“Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” states Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley. Even though this Gudvangen-located recreation village debuted a decade ago, Hylland witnessed a recent surge in visitors following this past summer’s FIFA World Cup, where Norway’s Erling Haaland popularized the Viking row as one of the catchiest celebrations of the football tournament.

It has been revealed that “We've seen significant growth in interest in Norway,” adds Nelson Oliveira, managing director, Nordics for luxury travel operator Abercrombie & Kent. Launched in 2024, their small group trip itineraries include a visit to the Viking Valley where guests interact with the Viking chieftain, dine in the reindeer-clad, candle-lit dining hall and visit the resident blacksmith, who continues to supply ironworks for the community, including door hinges and locks. “The Viking era is such an crucial part of Norway’s history, and we wanted to give guests an opportunity to experience that heritage beyond simply visiting a museum,” says Oliveira.

Magnus the blacksmith at Viking Valley.

Outside the village, quotidian Viking-inspired design is flourishing—and notably predates Haaland’s viral row chant. Matilde Brandt, marketing manager of Klesarven, a Viking heritage clothing retailer founded in 2015 by Lene Lorentzen, credits the global interest in historybounding—where elements of historical fashion are incorporated into everyday styles—for the spike in popularity of their Viking-inspired styles.

Sources indicate that “There is so much more to the [Viking] story than bearded men fighting and wearing dark colors,” says Brandt. Inspired by Hollywood’s enduringly maligned, inaccurate depictions of Viking Age Scandinavia, Klesarven focuses on historically accurate representations of the people living during that age. “Most of them were farmers, fishermen and craftspeople [who] wore bright, colorful clothing and were well put together,” says Brandt.

A Klesarven Frøya linen dress and Favn shawl.

These motifs are realized across Klesarven’s collection of wool sweaters, linen shirts, and riding skirts. One of Klesarven’s most popular designs is the Viking Age apron dress, inspired by a garment reserved for special occasions and ornamented with colorful beads, brooches, and jewelry crafted from silver, gold, and bronze. Women were also buried in these garments. “It keeps history alive,” says Brandt. “In this way, we help preserve old techniques and craftsmanship.”.

It has been revealed that preserving heritage is also a motivation of Runestone’s founders, Sonya and Kim Andre. Having both grown up on a stretch of coastline dotted with Viking history—Sonya from Uddevalla on Sweden’s west coast and her husband, Kim, from Halden, just across the Norwegian border—Runestone was born from a personal “obsession” with Viking culture.

According to recent reports, when the couple began building an online outfitter dedicated to Viking apparel, Norse jewelry, and rune wall art (the alphabet of Viking culture), Sonya recognized the bigger drive: “A lot of the brands out there lean into that ‘dressed up as a Viking’ look,” says Sonya. Runestone promises the opposite; born as a way to embrace history through a modern lens with designs, symbols, and styles as “something anyone can wear and connect with, not just a costume,” says Sonya.

In a recent development, “Every design has a real story behind it—a god, a creature, a rune, and we care a lot about getting that story right,” Sonya continues. “We’re carrying forward the spirit of the Vikings more than the actual lifestyle, religion, or the more brutal parts of the history.”.

Every week, Sonya receives emails, primarily from younger folks who are responding to the uptick in social media attention surrounding Viking culture. “They’re asking really specific questions,” she says, like inquiring about the gods—especially Odin, who is widely regarded as the god of wisdom and warfare—and requesting that Sonya point them toward reliable sources instead of pop culture tales.

For the curious travelers who make it to Norway, they have more opportunity than ever to engage with Viking heritage, from active opportunities like Viking Valley and shopping at Klesarven to passive participation at hotels.

In the northwestern Ålesund region, Storfjord Hotel was built in traditional Norwegian laft style with timber logs and turf roofs (the latter prioritized in Viking times for insulation). On Manshausen Island, located off the coast of northern Norway, the restaurant walls at the eponymous resort are covered with overlapping wooden scales built in the traditional Viking construction. Its groundskeeper team consists of two dozen sheep—an ancient Nordic breed that was kept during the Viking era.

“A hotel can become much more than a beautiful place to stay,” says Linda Gram Egede-Nissen, co-owner and CEO of interior design firm Gathe + Gram. “It can offer guests a subtle introduction to the culture and history of its surroundings.” In Trondheim, the northern city which served as the Viking capital of Norway many centuries ago, Gathe + Gram just completed the design blueprint for Eras, a boutique hotel where every room has its own distinctive name and story rooted in Viking history, mythology, or craftsmanship.

For this project, Gram Egede-Nissen was “particularly fascinated” by the “remarkable precision, complexity and beauty in the detailing” of historic jewelry from the Viking era. Her team translated the shapes, patterns, and proportions of spenne (buckles), skålspenne (ornamental brooches), and polyedrisk (beads) into architectural details and smaller design elements—decorative cushions, sculptural chandeliers, and wall art—throughout the interiors. “There is an incredible richness in the [Viking-era] jewelry—and many of these forms feel surprisingly relevant even today,” says Gram Egede-Nissen.

Industry observers note that “To me, that is where heritage becomes truly relevant,” adds Gram Egede-Nissen. “Not when we preserve it as something untouchable, but when we allow it to inspire new ideas.”.

The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.
  • Sources indicate that to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

Sources indicate that to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

In a recent development, if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Industry observers note that cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be remarked for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Recent findings suggest that yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

According to recent reports, and cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

Newly introduced in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

What I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the newly introduced era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

The Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly massive difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Industry observers note that other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

Sources indicate that an earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

In a recent development, what I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

Sources indicate that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Recent findings suggest that below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Recent findings suggest that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more important on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

Recent findings suggest that the other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

What I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

According to recent reports, 3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

Sources indicate that 6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

According to recent reports, I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Industry observers note that sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

According to recent reports, I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

Industry observers note that I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

In a recent development, heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a new name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8".

According to recent reports, people who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Industry observers note that another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and notes that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

According to recent reports, gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

It has been revealed that this skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of upcoming and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Recent findings suggest that ooni is a pizza oven firm, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

According to recent reports, this is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron upcoming wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being said, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no problems with sticking whatsoever.

In a recent development, this pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

The Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

We’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Recent findings suggest that anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

“Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

In a recent development, this is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

In a recent development, this is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic challenges, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Industry observers note that another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

Industry observers note that the seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

Recent findings suggest that when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

It has been revealed that no, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

In a recent development, if, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a substantial apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

How Am I Supposed to Survive the Apocalypse Without My Phone?
