📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors. It's a retro-style dessert with a hearty dose of seasonal cheer.

Industry observers note that I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them. One sweet treat that often finds its way onto our holiday brunch menus is a loaf (or three) of cranberry-orange bread. There’s just something so cozy about the combination of tart cranberries and sweet, bright orange juice—the inspiration for this cranberry crackle salad recipe.

Crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter). In this holiday-inspired crackle salad, the cream mixture is flavored with whole-berry cranberry sauce and orange zest. Fresh orange juice in the crackle adds a subtle citrus flavor, too. This recipe makes enough for a small crowd, and is perfect for sharing at a Thanksgiving potluck or as a fun throwback side dish at holiday gatherings.

Preheat the oven to 400°F. Line a 15x10x1-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

In a recent development, in a large bowl, stir together the broken pretzels, chopped pecans and brown sugar. Stir in the melted butter and orange juice to coat.

Spread the pretzel mixture in an even layer on the prepared baking sheet. Bake it for five to eight minutes or until it’s bubbly. Let it cool completely on the baking sheet before breaking it into pieces.

Editor’s Tip: Keep your eye on the crackle as it bakes; it can easily burn if baked too long.

It has been revealed that in a large bowl, beat together the softened cream cheese and vanilla. Stir in the cranberry sauce until it’s combined. Gently fold in the whipped topping until it’s incorporated.

In a recent development, fold in the orange zest. Cover the bowl and refrigerate the mixture for at least one hour.

Recent findings suggest that just before serving, stir in half of the pretzel mixture. Top the salad with the remaining pretzel mixture to serve. If you like, add sugared cranberries as an additional garnish.

Editor’s Tip: Avoid adding the crunch to the salad too early, as it will soften up over time.

Recent findings suggest that leftover cranberry crackle salad should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge. It will last for up to three days in the fridge. The crackle will soften over time once added to the salad.

Any extra crackle topping should be stored in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it crunchy. It should keep for up to one week.

Sources indicate that you can make the cream mixture and crackle up to two day in advance. Store the salad and crackle separately, and don’t combine them until just before serving the salad.

Sources indicate that if you want to dial up the crunch factor even more, allow the baked crackle to cool thoroughly before using it. This will ensure it has the crunchiest texture.

Fresh cranberries are a great option when they are in season. To make this cranberry crackle salad with fresh cranberries, you’ll need a 12-ounce package of whole cranberries. (You could also use frozen whole cranberries, but they need to thaw first.).

Sources indicate that in a food processor or blender, pulse the berries until they’re finely chopped. Pour the berries into a large bowl and stir in 1/2 cup of granulated sugar. Cover and refrigerate them for at least one hour or overnight. Use the fresh berry mixture in place of the canned cranberry sauce in this recipe.

This cranberry crackle salad will fit right in with any holiday potluck spread. It’s also a fun retro dessert salad to share at a holiday meal alongside classic savory offerings such as roasted turkey, mashed potatoes and green bean casserole.

The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

Sources indicate that the chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans swiftly filled the comments with condolences and support.

“Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

It has been revealed that others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve concerns or celebrate the wins,” he stated in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he said, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”.

And judging by the outpouring of love from fans, friends, and loved ones in the comments, the Fieri’s can take comfort knowing Jim left a lasting impression on more people than just his family.

Ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear. The turkey may be the centerpiece, but the side dishes are the real stars. “Thanksgiving is one of those meals where I care more about the sides than the main event!” she recently shared with her followers.

It has been revealed that in a recent Instagram post, Ina revealed that she’s especially excited to make several latest dishes from her latest cookbook, Simply Ina. There are familiar Thanksgiving favorites with a few clever twists, along with some store-bought shortcuts that prove even the Barefoot Contessa knows when to let someone else do part of the work. It’s a reassuring approach to a meal that can demand a lot of time in the kitchen.

Here’s a look at the six recipes Ina shared, along with similar Taste of Home dishes you can make for your own Thanksgiving dinner.

Industry observers note that ina’s combination of caramelized butternut squash and dried cranberries makes particularly good sense for Thanksgiving. Roasting brings out the squash’s natural sweetness, while the tart cranberries provide some welcome contrast. It’s a colorful alternative to the sweeter squash dishes that tend to find their way onto holiday tables, but one that wouldn’t look out of place next to a generous helping of Ina’s sausage and herb stuffing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Butternut Squash Jumble.

In a recent development, ina has always been a champion of making Thanksgiving easier, and her fresh turkey gravy takes that philosophy a step further. She’s starting with canned turkey gravy, then dressing it up for a richer, more homemade flavor. It’s a practical shortcut for someone who’s spent years teaching us how to make gravy from scratch. And as Ina points out, nobody wants leftover turkey without gravy, either. Making enough for Friday’s sandwiches is simply good planning.

Try a Taste of Home version: Make-Ahead Turkey Gravy.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that mashed potatoes are practically guaranteed a place on the Thanksgiving table, but Ina’s addition of garlic gives this familiar favorite a welcome savory kick. Ina actually starts with Bob Evans prepared mashed potatoes, then dresses them up with garlic confit, butter and half-and-half. With so many sweet, rich dishes competing for space on the plate, garlic mashed potatoes offer a little balance without sacrificing any of the buttery comfort everyone expects.

Try a Taste of Home version: Garlic Mashed Potatoes.

Recent findings suggest that brussels sprouts have come a long way from the boiled vegetables many of us remember from childhood, and Ina’s version pairs them with pecorino, a salty, sharp sheep’s milk cheese. The combination makes sense: The cheese adds richness and a savory bite that complements the sprouts’ slightly bitter flavor. It’s the sort of side dish that might even persuade a few longtime Brussels sprouts skeptics to reconsider.

Try a Taste of Home version: Brussels Sprouts with Garlic & Goat Cheese.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, here’s where Ina’s fondness for a good shortcut really comes into play. Her Chunky Cranberry Conserve starts with canned whole-berry cranberry sauce, which she dresses up with grated Granny Smith apple, orange juice and zest, raisins and pecans. The result has more texture and complexity than the contents of the can alone, without requiring you to start from scratch.

There’s something reassuring in knowing Ina Garten is perfectly content to open a can of cranberry sauce on Thanksgiving. If it’s good enough for Ina, the rest of us can probably stop apologizing for it.

Try a Taste of Home version: Cranberry-Apple Chutney.

In a recent development, sweet potatoes are a Thanksgiving staple, but Ina’s combination of maple syrup and chipotle gives them a welcome change of direction. The maple enhances their natural sweetness, while the smoky heat of chipotle keeps the dish firmly on the savory side of dinner.

And there’s another shortcut hiding in this dish. In a recent interview with Cup of Jo, Ina revealed that she uses prepared mashed sweet potatoes from Trader Joe’s, adding chipotle powder, maple syrup, butter and seasonings to make them her own. She figures nobody would know she hadn’t roasted the sweet potatoes herself, and with everything else that needs cooking on Thanksgiving, that’s a shortcut (and a great Trader Joe’s find) worth stealing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Hot Honey Sweet Potatoes.

#19903. Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

📅 16 Aug 2011 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these red-wine-braised short ribs have fans.
  • Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings.
  • Sources indicate that even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” claims one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Sources indicate that even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

What kind of short ribs should I buy?

Recent findings suggest that look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

Industry observers note that choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

Drawbridge Cabernet Sauvignon 2024.

Do I have to strain the vegetables?

For the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

How do I know when short ribs are done?

Start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

Industry observers note that yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and strategy every week with confidence. Download the app.

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Recent findings suggest that cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • Industry observers note that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

Industry observers note that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson.
  • From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.
  • Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

So, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s key to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she mentioned. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

It has been revealed that lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

Instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

It has been revealed that we’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson says not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she mentioned in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

Why Did My Pumpkin Pie Crack and How Can I Fix It?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.
  • Sources indicate that most cooking mistakes are fixable.
  • According to recent reports, pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.

Sources indicate that most cooking mistakes are fixable. When it comes to baking, though, one wrong move can ruin the whole recipe. It’s extra frustrating when you’re trying to make a Norman Rockwell-worthy pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, and a huge crack splits right through the center. Yes, you can still eat a cracked pumpkin pie, but if you can avoid the crack (or cover it up), all the better. The eyes eat first, as they say!

According to recent reports, pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes. Not to put the blame on one single ingredient, but it all comes down to the eggs—or, rather, how you treat them.

Pumpkin pie is technically a baked custard (like cheesecake), and eggs are thickeners in custards. Overbeating the eggs aerates the filling, which causes it to inflate during baking, then deflate and crack as it cools. Overbaking the filling will tighten the eggs and cause the filling to crack, too. And even if you pull the pie out at just the right moment, the filling can still crack from a rapid temperature change that makes the eggs contract. Ugh. It seems like there’s a lot working against you, but taking preemptive steps reduces your chances of ending up with a cracked pumpkin pie.

These are all the steps I take as a professional baker to reduce the risk of cracking, as well as a few tricks to cover up cracks if they appear.

Seasoned bakers know that whipping eggs aerates them. That’s usually a plus when you want structure in baking recipes, but in pumpkin pie, it’s the catalyst for a cracked filling. The pie’s filling will puff up in the oven, then promptly collapse as the eggs deflate. That structural change causes the filling to crack. It’s the same problem that leads to a cracked cheesecake!

Room-temperature eggs blend into custards much more easily, so take the eggs out of the fridge 30 to 60 minutes before starting, depending on the kitchen temperature. Once you add the eggs to the filling, mix them just until they’re combined.

Even if you use a reliable pumpkin pie recipe with tons of five-star reviews (cough, cough: our pumpkin pie recipe) and follow it to the very letter, it may be the oven that betrays you in the end.

Ovens often have miscalibrated internal thermometers, so even if you set your oven to the recommended 350°F, the real temperature may be significantly higher. Before you realize it, the pumpkin pie is overbaked and already cracked.

Buy an oven thermometer and hang it from one of the oven racks for all your bakes going forward. They usually cost about $10—totally worth the investment!

In a recent development, have you ever read a recipe with specific oven rack placements? They’re not there as a suggestion; oven rack placement significantly affects your bake. Ovens produce heat from the bottom, and this creates zones as that heat rises: hotter on top and cooler down below.

Recent findings suggest that since you want your pumpkin pie to bake relatively low and slow, the bottom oven rack is best. The filling cooks evenly, and the pie crust browns beautifully—no cracks and no soggy bottom.

Recent findings suggest that the best way to avoid an overbaked (and therefore cracked) pumpkin pie is to know the signs of doneness. The edges should dome a bit, but the center should be wobbly like Jell-O, not rippling like an ocean wave. The pumpkin pie will continue to bake from the residual heat once the oven is off.

Industry observers note that this is where your oven light comes in handy. Don’t open the oven door until you see the edges start to dome, or cool air will rush inside before it’s supposed to. Only when you see the dome should you check for a wobbly center.

Even after meticulously following every single step to avoid a pumpkin pie crack, a rapid change in temperature can undo all that hard work. The shock of removing a pumpkin pie from a hot oven and setting down in a cold November kitchen (or, worse, a 32° fridge) will cause the eggs to contract, leading to a crack.

Recent findings suggest that once the pie is done baking, turn the oven off and leave the door slightly ajar. If the oven door doesn’t stay open on its own, prop it open with a wooden spoon. Keep the pie in the oven until it’s completely cooled.

Industry observers note that so, your pumpkin pie did crack. That’s OK! It happens from time to time, even when you follow all the rules. The good news is that the pie still tastes great. Even better? You can cover up the crack with homemade whipped cream. Pile it in the center or pipe it in a decorative pattern. Use stabilized whipped cream if you want to add the topping a day ahead of time. You can even grate fresh nutmeg on top for dimension.

Recent findings suggest that you can do the same with Swiss meringue. Spread it simply, or pipe it on top for a substantial, showy decoration. Toast the meringue so it’s beautifully golden brown.

Breaking: Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (466 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
  • In a recent development, the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • According to recent reports, most recipes serve multiple people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

In a recent development, the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

According to recent reports, most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Industry observers note that slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Latest Update: Is Cottage Cheese Good for You?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yes, cottage cheese is good for you!
  • In a recent development, I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral.
  • As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Yes, cottage cheese is good for you! It's packed with protein and calcium, but the kind you buy matters. Here's how to choose the best cottage cheese for cooking, baking and snacking.

In a recent development, I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral. TikTok trends have turned this humble dairy staple into everything from high-protein flatbread to better-for-you ice cream. Packed with protein and crucial vitamins and minerals, cottage cheese is an easy way to make everyday meals more satisfying.

As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals. There are so many creative ways to use cottage cheese, and a whole upcoming world of options opens up when you whip it smooth. Think: smoothies, creamy dips, pasta sauces, puddings and more!

But as versatile as cottage cheese is, you can’t swap it into every recipe without a little know-how. And with so many milkfat options, the one you buy matters. I’ll share my favorite ways to use it, which varieties work best for different dishes and a few tricks to help you get delicious results every time.

First things first: Here’s why you might want to toss another tub of cottage cheese into your grocery cart.

In a recent development, cottage cheese is one of my go-to high-protein foods. A half-cup serving packs 12 to 14 grams of protein, roughly the same amount you’d get from two large eggs.

Industry observers note that adding a scoop of cottage cheese to my plate is an easy way to make meals and snacks more satisfying without turning on the stove. I especially like it at breakfast, when it’s all too easy to end up with a meal that’s heavy on carbohydrates but light on protein. A scoop alongside toast and fruit, or blended into pancake batter, gives breakfast a little extra staying power without much effort.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to be lifting heavy weights to care about muscle health. Our bodies need plenty of protein to maintain and repair muscle tissue, and that becomes especially key as we get older.

Recent findings suggest that I like to keep cottage cheese on hand for an easy post-workout snack because there’s nothing to prep. Pair it with fruit or whole-grain crackers, and you’ve got protein plus carbohydrates to help muscles refuel and recover after exercise.

Industry observers note that the protein in cottage cheese does more than help keep you full and support your muscles—it also plays an crucial role in keeping your bones strong. Cottage cheese aprovides two minerals that work together to support bone health: phosphorus and calcium.

It’s worth noting that cottage cheese contains less calcium than a serving of milk or Greek yogurt, but it can absolutely contribute to your daily intake. Just be sure to include other calcium-rich foods in your diet, too.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that the type of cottage cheese you buy can make a big difference in how your recipes turn out. Like other dairy products, cottage cheese comes in different milkfat percentages, which affects its taste and texture.

In a recent development, I usually reach for 2% or 4% cottage cheese, depending on how I’m using it. Low-fat (2% cottage cheese) is perfect for whipping into dips, spreads and pasta sauces. It contains enough fat to blend smooth and creamy without feeling too heavy.

According to recent reports, full-fat, or 4% cottage cheese, gets my vote for baked goods, casseroles and lasagna fillings. The extra fat adds richness, which is especially helpful if you’re using it in place of sour cream or cream cheese.

According to recent reports, I usually skip fat-free cottage cheese for cooking. It tends to be watery with a slightly chalky taste, and the lack of fat can make creamy recipes less satisfying. That extra moisture can also affect the texture of baked dishes, so I prefer cottage cheese with a little more fat for the best results.

Recent findings suggest that for all its nutritional perks, cottage cheese can also pack a lot of sodium. Some brands contain more than 400 milligrams per half-cup serving. Eat a full cup, and you could be getting more than 800 milligrams of sodium (about one-third of the recommended daily limit) from cottage cheese alone.

Too much sodium can raise blood pressure and increase your risk of heart disease, so it’s worth paying attention to how much you’re getting, especially if you eat cottage cheese regularly.

It has been revealed that if you’re watching your sodium intake, compare labels and choose a brand that’s lower in sodium. Good Culture is one of my favorite cottage cheese brands. With 380 milligrams of sodium per serving, it’s a little lower than other brands.

I also go easy on added salt when using cottage cheese with salty ingredients like Parmesan or ranch seasoning.

Julia Hartbeck for Taste of Home.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

Recent findings suggest that these impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Sources indicate that ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

Recent findings suggest that this pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

Sources indicate that for some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

In a recent development, give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

There’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a massive crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

It has been revealed that A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

It will be a miracle if this colorful, festive and irresistibly sweet Hanukkah bark lasts for eight days and eight nights.

In a recent development, every holiday is sweeter with a tray of festive chocolate bark—and Hanukkah is no exception! This 30-minute Hanukkah bark recipe takes just a handful of ingredients and turns them into the perfect treat for sharing with friends and family as you celebrate the Festival of Lights. The surface is swirled (a lot like our marbled almond roca), and it looks as if a few dreidels were sent spinning over the melted blue candy melts and white chocolate.

It has been revealed that A tray of Hanukkah bark, decorated with an eye-catching array of colorful and shimmering sprinkles, makes a showstopping centerpiece for any Hanukkah dessert table. But it can also be a thoughtful homemade food gift you can pack into tins with a handful of chocolate gelt.

Line a 15x10x1-inch sheet pan with parchment paper.

Add the blue and white candy melts to separate microwave-safe glass bowls, then microwave at 50% power in 30-second increments, stirring after each, until smooth.

Editor’s Tip: If you’re worried about your chocolate setting too swiftly, place the sheet pan in a warm oven while preparing the candy melts. A warm (but not hot) sheet pan keeps the candy melts fluid while you work, making them easier to swirl without the pressure to rush.

In a recent development, dollop alternating spoonfuls of each color onto the parchment paper in a checkerboard pattern, leaving space between spoonfuls. Use an offset spatula to merge the colors together, then smooth them to a 1/4-inch thickness. Use a knife or wooden skewer to swirl them to create a marbled look.

Immediately sprinkle the candy melts with candy-coated chocolates and assorted sprinkles.

Transfer the pan to the refrigerator and chill the bark until it’s set. Break it into large pieces.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Store Hanukkah bark in an airtight container at room temperature for one to three weeks.

Absolutely! Hanukkah bark is a great make-ahead treat for the holiday season because it can be stored at room temperature and has a longer shelf life than many other Hanukkah desserts.

Yes, Hanukkah bark freezes well. Break it apart, then store it in an airtight, freezer-safe container for three to six months. Enjoy it straight from the freezer or defrost it at room temperature.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a recent development, white chocolate and candy melts can be finicky and prone to seizing if you warm them too swiftly or at too high a temperature. If using a microwave, warm them gently on a low power setting in short increments for the best results. If you’re nervous, you can melt them on the stovetop using a double boiler or a heat-safe bowl set over a saucepan filled with 1 to 2 inches of water. If neither of those suits you, using a slow cooker or a water bath are some other ways to melt chocolate.

Yes, you can dye white chocolate. Use an oil-based or powdered type of food coloring for the best results. Gel and traditional food dyes contain too much water, which will cause the white chocolate to seize and become grainy.

In a recent development, for the most eye-catching look, choose an array of sprinkles with different sizes and shapes. Varying pearl and jimmie sprinkle sizes, paired with specialty sprinkles shaped like stars, menorahs or dreidels add visual interest to the bark.

Recent findings suggest that while gelt looks attractive on Hanukkah bark, foil-wrapped chocolates are difficult to remove and unwrap once they’ve been adhered to the bark. If you want to add gelt, unwrap the pieces before arranging them on the bark.

You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint.
  • Frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option.
  • Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. And the most involved, time-consuming dish is undoubtedly the turkey. The centerpiece of your holiday table needs hours in the oven and at least a day of brining, but don't forget the time it takes to defrost beforehand, too.

Frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option. But they do require a little extra TLC and planning. So if you buy a frozen bird this year, you'll need to know how to work with it.

Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely. Like chicken, turkey can spread Salmonella and other harmful bacteria. You should exercise caution at every stage of the process, including thawing, to avoid making your guests sick. Here’s what you should know.

Sources indicate that the USDA indicates it's also safe to defrost turkey in cold water, but in our opinion, it's not worth the hassle. The best bet is to thaw it in the refrigerator, where the bird can gradually defrost at the safe temperature with less risk of bacterial growth. What you should never do: thaw it on the counter, in the garage, or with warm water.

These environments are less controlled and can expose the turkey to the temperature danger zone (between 40°F and 140°F), where germs grow rapidly. Even if the center of the turkey is still frozen, the thawed exterior can become a hotbed for Salmonella by the time you're ready to roast.

Recent findings suggest that roasted turkey drippings make great gravy. But raw turkey juice dripping all over your fridge? Not so much. Even shrink-wrapped birds can leak, so you should always store your turkey on a baking sheet or roasting pan while it thaws.

It has been revealed that food safety experts also recommend storing raw meat on the lowest shelf. That way, any leaks are less likely to drip onto other ingredients in your fridge.

According to recent reports, we know you're probably keeping a lot of other ingredients in your fridge, so it can be hard to set aside extra room for the turkey. That remarked, it's a step worth doing. Giving your turkey plenty of personal space minimizes the risk of raw meat or its juices coming into contact with other ingredients.

In the event that your turkey does contaminate another ingredient, here's what to know: Foods that won’t be cooked, like salad greens, should be tossed if they’ve come into contact with raw turkey juices. Cooking contaminated foods thoroughly can kill harmful bacteria, but you’ll also need to clean any surfaces the juices touched.

Recent findings suggest that turkeys are major, so they take a long time to thaw all the way through. The experts at Butterball say you should allocate a day for every four pounds of turkey if you're keeping it in the fridge. That means if you're working with a 16-pound bird, set aside four days just for defrosting. Once it's fully thawed, Butterball says your turkey will stay safe in the fridge for up to four days.

And on top of that, brining can make your turkey even more flavorful. If your frozen bird didn’t come pre-seasoned, consider setting aside another day or two for that step. (Want some guidance? Check out our brining guide.).

Industry observers note that it’s extremely crucial to keep things clean while you’re handling a turkey. One of the most common ways Salmonella spreads in the kitchen is through cross-contamination caused by poor hygiene.

Industry observers note that so wash those hands (including under your fingernails!) with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Make sure you also thoroughly clean any utensils and surfaces that come into contact with raw turkey or its juices using hot, soapy water.

According to recent reports, and above all, don’t stress! Americans prepare millions of turkeys every Thanksgiving, so you're not alone in your turkey-roasting journey. Follow the tips above to ensure yours turns out safe to eat and delicious.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that there are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy.
  • According to recent reports, making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It only takes a splash to give homemade gravy the rich, savory flavor you're after.

It has been revealed that there are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy. Everyone seems to have a preferred method, a secret ingredient or a little trick they’ve been using for years. My mom has always sworn by Kitchen Bouquet, a seasoning sauce that gives gravy a little color and kick of flavor. I’m fairly certain she’s had the same bottle since the Reagan administration, and that it only comes out of the cupboard on Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky. Even with plenty of turkey drippings and a well-made stock, sometimes it needs a little something extra. Over the years, I’ve experimented with all sorts of ways to give my gravy more flavor, but the one I come back to every time is an ingredient I always have in my pantry.

I’ve been adding a splash of soy sauce to my gravy for years, and it’s one of those little tricks that makes a noticeable difference without anyone being able to put their finger on why.

Industry observers note that soy sauce is rich in umami, the deeply savory flavor that makes foods like mushrooms, Parmesan cheese and the golden crust of a steak so satisfying. Adding a little soy sauce to gravy enhances those same savory flavors, giving it a richness that might otherwise require a longer cooking time. It doesn’t make your gravy taste like soy sauce, provided you use a light hand. It just makes it taste more like really good gravy.

Worcestershire sauce is another popular addition that works for much the same reason, bringing its own combination of savory flavor, acidity and a hint of sweetness. I’ve tried plenty of different additions over the years, and while they all have their merits, soy sauce remains my favorite. I love the depth it brings without competing with the flavors of the turkey and stock.

According to recent reports, the trick with soy sauce is knowing when to add it and, perhaps most importantly, when to stop. You’re not trying to introduce a new flavor to your gravy so much as coax a little more out of what’s already there. If someone can identify soy sauce in the finished product, you’ve probably been a bit too generous.

Recent findings suggest that I always add mine at the end, once the gravy has thickened and I’m happy with the consistency. Start with about a teaspoon for every two cups of gravy, stir it in, and give it a taste. Depending on the stock and drippings you’ve used, that may be all you need. If not, add a little more, tasting as you go.

One thing worth remembering is that soy sauce is salty. Very salty, in fact, so save your final seasoning adjustments until after you’ve added it. This is particularly notable if you’re using store-bought stock, which may already contain plenty of sodium. Reduced-sodium soy sauce is an option, too, but I generally use the regular stuff and adjust accordingly.

In a recent development, and don’t save this trick for Thanksgiving! It works beautifully in beef and chicken gravy, too, especially when the pan drippings aren’t quite as flavorful as you’d hoped. A splash of soy sauce won’t make up for a badly made gravy, but it can do an impressive amount of work for an otherwise perfectly respectable one.

Have you used soy sauce in gravy before? Let us know in the comments below!

  • The best for all varieties of air fryer needers are below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens that circulate hot air around your food. Our years of testing air fryers (and we’ve used over two dozen in that time) have taught us that there are plenty out there that can give you crispy-enough results—but the very best air fryers churn out not only golden brown french fries and crispy-skinned chicken wings, but tender fillets of salmon and even whole roast chickens at the touch of a button.

According to recent reports, air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality. Some even dehydrate and steam too. And most recently more bowl-style air fryers have started to hit shelves, which swap a slide-in basket for a glass container and top-down, air-frying lid.

The best for all varieties of air fryer needers are below.

It has been revealed that fresh in this patch: We tested five models in the growing category of glass air fryers, i.e., those with slide-in glass baskets or glass bowl bases with an air fryer lid. This included new reviews for air fryers from Cuisinart, Chefman, Kisimile, and Magnifique, plus retesting the Ninja Crispi against this new crop of similar products.

Most air fryers fit into one of three categories: oven, basket, or bowl.

A countertop convection oven, or air fryer–toaster oven, combines most of the crisping power of the basket-style air fryers you know and love with the multifunctionality you get from a toaster oven or countertop oven. Generally, the “air frying” function is achieved with a perforated slide-in rack, which usually means lots of cooking surface, but the racks are usually shallow and can require careful tossing or flipping of whatever you’re cooking, depending on the dish. But air fryer ovens, like the Breville Smart Oven Pro with its 13 different cooking modes, can do a lot, making them bona fide do-it-all kitchen appliances.

It has been revealed that basket-style air fryers aren’t as versatile as air fryer ovens, but they’re also less expensive and take up less space. They also tend to deliver better final results on traditional air fryer stuff like crisping up small foods that require shaking (tater tots, french fries, or brussels sprouts), for which a handled basket is far easier to maneuver. Minuses are that they can be hard to clean and limited on square inches inside the basket. They’re also sometimes made of plastic or nonstick coated materials, which may not appeal to some consumers.

Bowl air fryers offer some of the best (and worst) of both worlds and also some unique benefits. Most of these include a heat-resistant glass bowl acting as the basket. Some models operate much like basket air fryers, with the glass container sliding into the base unit, while others opt for a “lid” that sits on top and houses the air frying mechanism. The glass baskets make these very easy to clean (included crisping trays are another story), however their functionality for shaking and pausing to flip foods can be cumbersome. But many come with lids for the glass containers, letting them double as prep and storage containers too.

According to recent reports, what we love: The 6-Quart Cosori Turboblaze Smart Air Fryer impressed us in every test, producing evenly browned and crispy frozen sweet potato fries, juicy chicken breasts, and perfectly cooked brussels sprouts. It has a straightforward digital interface that allows you to easily set the time and temperature and an impressive array of preset programs (Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep Warm).

In a recent development, A few things set the Turboblaze apart from the competition (including the previous longtime winner of this test, the Instant Vortex Slim). Most notably, it consistently produced the crispiest food of any air fryer we tested in record time. That may have something to do with the fact that there’s more space between the crisper plate (where the food sits) and the bottom of the basket than there is in some of the other top-performing models we’ve tried, which allows for better air circulation.

Another standout feature is its variable fan speeds, which adjust automatically depending on the cooking function. Air Fry, for example, is one of four “turbo modes,” running the fan at full blast (speed 5), while Bake uses a gentler speed 3 to avoid disrupting delicate foods. Low-temperature settings like Dehydrate and Proof drop all the way down to speed 1.

The model we tested includes smart features, meaning you can control it remotely or use voice commands via the VeSync app. If that’s not your thing, Cosori also sells a non-smart version for about $10 less.

What we’d leave: Our gripes with this model are minor. It’s slightly annoying that you have to press a release button to pull the basket out. And while the greater amount of space between the crisper tray and basket bottom contributes to better airflow (and thus better browning), it means food is more likely to fall through while cooking.

If you’re on a tighter budget, have very little counter space to spare, or are mostly crisping up food just for yourself, consider the Cosori Lite 2.1-Quart Mini Air Fryer.

It has been revealed that what we love: This compact air fryer did a beautiful job crisping and browning small servings of frozen tater tots and fries, sliced zucchini, and veggie burger patties (two at a time, max). Depending on where you buy, it will only costs $50–$60 (as of publish time)—not at all bad for a lightweight, quiet, digital air fryer with four easy-to-use presets (air-fry, roast, bake, and reheat). It’s easy to tuck into a cabinet and to clean. Like the Cosori Blaze, the Lite has a nonstick basket. It also won’t remind you when it’s time to shake your food, so you’ll need to keep an eye on the timer yourself (luckily, the digital display makes this pretty easy).

It has been revealed that if you want an air fryer with maximum versatility and have some counter space to spare, spring for the Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro. Breville makes a few different models (which can be found in the kitchens of many of our editors), but this one is the best combination of performance and value.

What we love: This midrange model has been our top pick for years now because of its versatility, build quality, intuitive design, and consistently strong performance in testing.

In testing, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro delivered reliably great results. It excelled at foods that need to be laid in a flat, even layer across the crisper tray (think veggie burgers or salmon fillets), but also handled frozen fries, tots, and sweet potato fries well. Its interior is roomy enough to fit a quarter sheet pan or 13x9" casserole pan, which means it can effectively double your oven space (or eliminate the need to turn on your full-size oven altogether).

This model is also a favorite among BA staffers and Test Kitchen editors, as well as award-winning cookbook author Nik Sharma, who developed some of BA’s favorite air fryer recipes. “I prefer toaster-oven-style to basket-style air fryers, because they’re easier to use for more common tasks like baking, toasting bread, and roasting more efficiently,” Sharma notes.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: As with most oven-style air fryers, it’s harder to toss or shake small foods mid-cook compared to a basket-style machine. We also found that, in general, food benefited from a higher cooking temperature (and often slightly longer cook time) relative to the basket-style winners.

If you like the idea of going the air fryer–toaster oven route but (1) don’t have the space for the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro or (2) don’t want to shell out $400 in pursuit of crispiness, here’s some good news: Breville offers the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact, which is essentially a smaller, cheaper version of our top pick.

There are fewer niche modes than the Pro—no Dehydrate or Proof—but it does include four air-frying-specific presets in addition to a standard Air Fry setting.

We found using the Compact intuitive (the guide printed on the inside of the oven door helped). We also appreciated the “bit more” button, a feature borrowed from Breville’s toasters that adds a touch of extra cooking time when your fries are looking just a touch underdone.

We still prefer the larger model for its versatility and additional functionality, but this little oven would make a worthy addition to any smaller kitchen.

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: While the Compact did well in most tests, it struggled a bit with frozen sweet potato fries. This largely came down to overcrowding due to the smaller capacity: While we tried to fit an entire bag’s worth on a single tray, the unevenness with which the fries browned is a good example of the fact that, unlike a basket fryer, countertop oven-style air fryers are best used to cook things in a single layer.

As mentioned, there’s a guide to oven inserts and placement on the inside of the oven’s door, but this is easy to miss, and these suggestions did not appear in full in the manual.
